client: Lately I've been feeling really distant from my friends, even though I know they're trying to be supportive. It's been six months since my mom passed, but when they talk about getting together or going out, it just makes me angry - like they've already forgotten how much I'm hurting. I don't know if talking about this will help when the pain just feels so... permanent.
therapist: I hear how deeply you're hurting, and it makes sense that you'd feel distant when others don't seem to fully grasp the weight of your grief. Have you noticed any particular thoughts that come up when friends suggest spending time together?

client: Yeah, I keep thinking "they just don't get it" when they invite me places. Like if they really understood, they wouldn't be acting so... normal? It's like my whole world stopped but theirs just kept going. That's what makes me so angry - how can they just move on like nothing happened?
therapist: It sounds like there's a real disconnect between your experience and how you perceive theirs, which must feel incredibly isolating. I wonder if part of the anger comes from wishing they could better understand this profound shift in your life? What do you imagine it would feel like if they acknowledged that your world has changed in a way theirs hasn't?

client: I guess if they acknowledged it more openly, I wouldn't feel so alone in this. But part of me thinks even if they did, it wouldn't change how empty everything feels now. It's like... their words wouldn't bring her back, so what's the point of them trying?
therapist: That deep sense of emptiness and longing is so valid—no words can fill the space your mom left, and that reality is incredibly painful to sit with. I hear you wrestling with two truths: wanting connection while also feeling like nothing can truly help right now—what's that tension like for you in this moment?

client: It's exhausting, honestly. One minute I'm craving someone to just sit with me in this pain, and the next I'm pushing everyone away because their presence just reminds me that no one will ever understand like she did. It feels like I'm stuck between wanting comfort and rejecting it at the same time.
therapist: That push-and-pull makes so much sense—you're yearning for the kind of understanding only your mom could provide, while also needing human connection in your grief. How does it feel when you notice yourself caught in that cycle between reaching out and withdrawing?

client: It makes me feel even more alone, honestly. Like I'm failing at grief because I can't just pick one way to be - either fully open or fully closed off. And then I get mad at myself for being so inconsistent with people who are trying to care.
therapist: It sounds like you're holding yourself to really high expectations about how grief "should" look, when in reality, it's often messy and inconsistent—and that's completely okay. What might it feel like to offer yourself the same compassion you'd give a friend going through this?

client: I don't know if I can be that gentle with myself. When I imagine a friend going through this, of course I'd tell them to take all the time they need. But for me? It feels weak to need that much time. Like I should be stronger by now.
therapist: That difference in standards you're holding for yourself versus others is so telling—it sounds like you're carrying an extra layer of pain through self-judgment. Where do you think that belief comes from, that grief should have an expiration date when it comes to your own healing?

client: I guess it comes from feeling like I'm supposed to be "functional" again—like I'm letting people down by not bouncing back. Everyone keeps asking when I'll feel normal again, and their questions make me feel like I'm taking too long... even though I know grief doesn't just stop on a schedule.
therapist: It makes so much sense that others' expectations would make this even harder—you're already carrying the grief, and now there's this pressure to perform recovery too. I wonder what it might feel like to gently challenge the idea that being "functional" means needing less time to grieve?

client: It feels impossible to untangle those two things. Like if I accept needing more time, I'm admitting I'll never really be okay again. I think part of me is afraid that if I stop performing "better," people will stop checking in altogether, and then I'll be completely alone with this.
therapist: That fear of being abandoned in your grief is so understandable—it sounds like you're caught between protecting yourself and risking deeper connection. What would it be like to share even a small piece of this worry with someone you trust?

client: I think about telling my best friend this sometimes, but then I chicken out because what if it makes things awkward? What if she doesn't know what to say and then just... stops calling? The risk feels too big when I'm barely holding it together as it is.
therapist: It sounds like there's a lot at stake for you in sharing this—you're already feeling vulnerable, and the fear of losing that connection if she doesn't respond "right" is so real. I wonder if there might be a middle ground, like sharing just a small piece of this with her and seeing how she responds?

client: I guess I could try... but even the thought of bringing it up makes my stomach twist. What if I open up and she doesn't know what to say? Or worse, what if she tries to fix it with some platitude like "time heals all wounds"? That just makes me feel even more misunderstood.
therapist: That fear of being met with clichés instead of real understanding is completely valid—it sounds like you're craving responses that truly honor the depth of your pain. I wonder if it might help to share what kind of support you're actually hoping for from her? For example, letting her know you don't need fixing—just someone to listen without solutions?
